Maya — thanks for the clear asks. Attached is our completed worksheet (Altavista_RFI_Worksheet_20260520.xlsx) plus a short assumptions doc. Key points up front:

1) Recommended GPU mix (initial reserve):
   - 40% H100 (4x80GB) nodes for large-chat / long-context summarization models (LLM family: redwood-24b / open-30b equivalents).
   - 40% A100-80GB nodes for general purpose generation and medium models (12–20B).
   - 20% L4 / L40s or equivalent for high-concurrency embedders and lightweight rerankers.

2) Precision & quantization profiles:
   - We support int8 and 4-bit quantized variants in production; recommended starting profile: int8 for generation models to balance quality and throughput.
   - For the 24B/30B class where quality is critical, we recommend mixed-precision: KV cache stays fp16 for fidelity, while matmuls use int8 kernels.

3) Throughput & latency assumptions (reserved pool targets):
   - Reserved pool target: 40% of current traffic => ~480k requests/day.
   - Baseline steady-state concurrency: ~2.5k concurrent inferences across the pool during peak windows.
   - Latency SLO (reserved lanes): 95th percentile generation latency <120ms per request (for short-turn prompts ~64–128 tokens), 99th <200ms with configured tail capacity and local prefix caching.

4) Burst lanes and autoscaling interaction:
   - Reserved pools are capacity-guaranteed up to committed vGPU slots; autoscaling can expand with a dedicated burst pool subject to burst bandwidth policy.
   - For deterministic tail latency we recommend a 10% reserved buffer and a pre-warmed burst lane that can be used for non-reserved traffic. When the burst lane is used, reserved requests remain on prioritized nodes and are not preempted.

5) Operational controls and rollout:
   - Canary rollouts by route/model, automatic fallback to a quantized variant if latency breach detected.
   - Prefix/KV caching for clinical templates and repeated patient prompts to reduce token compute by up to 35% in our measurements.

I've annotated the attached worksheet with per-endpoint vGPU slot estimates, node counts, and cost buckets. See page 'Assumptions' in Redwood_Sizing_Assumptions_20260521.pdf for the model-to-GPU mapping.

Next steps: if this aligns with your expectations we can propose two commitment options (12mo and 36mo) and a pilot window for 30 days of monitored traffic. I can join a technical sync with Eng Ops Monday if that helps.

Best,

Maya / Eng Ops — attaching the updated worksheet and assumptions with in-line answers to your Eng Ops questions. Highlights:

- Co-location / noisy neighbors: Redwood's scheduler supports soft-packing for low-util windows; embedders can co-reside on L40s with generator vGPUs on H100/A100 nodes only when explicit packing rules are set. By default reserved pools use isolation policies (no co-located non-reserved containers) to guarantee tail latency.
- Model pinning / fallback: We will honor per-route "no-automatic-fallback" if requested; operationally this means if a model OOMs or an instance fails we will preserve the route on the committed variant and route overflow to a logically separate fallback pool only if you enable it. We'll add a contract addendum that specifies SLA credits for failures in pinned routes.
- Warm-up strategy: pre-warm 20% of the reserved nodes 30 minutes before expected peak windows (can be automated by a cron-like schedule) and enable prefix cache warm-up from production snapshots — typical warm-up reduces token compute latency by ~25% in our pilots.

Proposal: two commitment options included in the attached Draft_12mo_Commitment_Tiers.xlsx — a 12-month baseline and a 36-month more favorable tier. Pilot details, deliverables, and the DocuSign link are included.

Proposed next steps:
1) Confirm pilot start window (we have availability on 2026-06-07).
2) Sign mutual NDA addendum + commitment to baseline 12mo pilot (counter-signed DocuSign link below).
3) Schedule Eng Ops deep-dive with our SRE runbook owners (30–45 min).
